key_terms.meaning: The single stack of function frames Node's one JavaScript thread is running; anything sitting on it blocks everything else.
The loop that repeatedly asks the operating system what finished, then pushes those callbacks onto the call stack, phase by phase.
Event loop phase that runs callbacks whose setTimeout or setInterval delay has expired.
Event loop phase where Node waits for completed I/O and runs the matching callbacks; it blocks here when nothing else is ready.
Event loop phase that runs setImmediate callbacks immediately after the poll phase.
Project manifest holding name, scripts and dependency version ranges such as "express": "^4.18.2".
Lockfile recording the exact version and download URL of every installed package, so npm ci gives the same tree everywhere.
^1.4.2 means ≥1.4.2 and <2.0.0; ~1.4.2 means ≥1.4.2 and <1.5.0; 1.4.2 means that exact version only.
A channel that moves data in small chunks instead of one big buffer, so memory stays flat and work starts early.
readable.pipe(writable) forwards each chunk and ends the destination, but it does not forward errors to the destination.
Node's on(event, listener) and emit(event, args) pattern; fs streams, http servers and your own objects all use it.
A function (req, res, next) registered with app.use that runs in order and either calls next() or sends the response.
Built-in middleware that serves every file in a folder directly, with no route written for it.
An API style where a URL names a resource (/books/7) and the HTTP method names the action on it.
A reusable set of open MySQL connections; pool.query() borrows one, runs the SQL, and returns it to the pool.
A slot in an SQL string whose value is bound separately, so user input is data and never becomes SQL code.
MongoDB's row equivalent (a BSON document, no fixed schema) stored inside a collection, the table equivalent.
A signed token of the form header.payload.signature; the server checks the signature and trusts the payload without a lookup.
Cross-site scripting: attacker JavaScript runs inside your page's origin because your page printed untrusted input.
The image is a frozen filesystem plus startup command built from a Dockerfile; the container is one running instance of it.

takeaways: Node is fast because a single JavaScript thread never waits: files, network and timers go to the operating system and come back as callbacks.
package.json holds the version ranges you asked for; package-lock.json holds the exact versions you actually got, and only the lockfile makes installs repeatable.
Streams beat readFile for large data because chunks flow through with flat memory, and pipe() alone will not report a failure of the source.
In Express the request walks a fixed, ordered chain of middleware until one function sends a response or calls next(err).
REST is a naming discipline: URLs are nouns, HTTP methods are verbs, status codes are the result, and JSON is the body format.
SQL safety comes from ? placeholders that bind values separately; string concatenation is what turns user text into executable code.
MongoDB swaps tables for collections and rows for schemaless documents, and a query is just a filter document each candidate must match.
Sessions keep the proof on the server behind a cookie id; a JWT keeps the proof in a signed token on the client and cannot be revoked easily.
XSS defeats any token stored in localStorage; HttpOnly cookies keep the credential out of reach of injected script.
Docker fixes the environment, CI/CD fixes the human step, and together they make a deploy the same repeatable command every time.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always ask you to describe a mechanism and then show code: the event loop phases, the middleware order, a CRUD route set, a pooled SQL query, a Mongo filter, and an authentication flow are the standard set.

bank.q: Explain the Node.js event loop. Name its phases in order and state exactly what runs in each.
outline: Single JS thread plus libuv handles async work
Phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, close
microtasks (promises) drain between phases
poll blocks when no timers are due and no I/O is ready
consequence: never block the stack or every client waits

bank.q: Distinguish package.json from package-lock.json. What exactly does npm install when it sees ^4.17.1 and when it sees ~4.17.1?
outline: manifest vs lockfile
dependencies vs devDependencies
semver caret and tilde ranges with the upper bound
npm install may update the lockfile, npm ci installs it exactly
commit the lockfile for reproducible builds

bank.q: What is middleware in Express? Describe the order in which application-level, router-level, built-in and error-handling middleware execute, and how next() controls the flow.
outline: signature (req, res, next)
registration order equals execution order
next() passes on, next('route') skips, next(err) jumps to error middleware
four-argument error handler placed last
res.send ends the chain

bank.q: Define REST and show how the HTTP methods map to CRUD operations on a /books collection, including the status codes each should return.
outline: resources as nouns, methods as verbs
statelessness and uniform interface
GET /books and GET /books/7 with 200 and 404
POST /books with 201 and Location header
PUT and PATCH, DELETE with 204
idempotency of GET, PUT, DELETE

bank.q: Write an Express application that serves a public folder as static files and exposes GET, POST, PUT and DELETE routes on /books backed by an in-memory array, returning correct status codes and JSON bodies.
outline: express() and app.use(express.json())
app.use(express.static('public'))
route parameters req.params.id
validation returning 400
201 on create, 404 when the id is missing, 204 on delete
listen on process.env.PORT

bank.q: Write a Node program that copies a 2 GB file using fs.createReadStream and fs.createWriteStream with pipe(). Explain what happens if the source fails and how to fix it.
outline: chunked transfer, flat memory
pipe() forwards data and calls end() on destination
errors on the readable are not forwarded by pipe alone
attach 'error' on each stream or use stream.pipeline / finished
destroy the destination so no half-written file is left

bank.q: Using mysql2 with a connection pool, write code to create a table, insert a row with placeholders, select rows, update one row and delete one row. Show how the result objects are used.
outline: mysql.createPool with host, user, password, database
pool.query(sql, values, callback) or the promise API
CREATE TABLE with a primary key
INSERT with ? placeholders and an array of values
SELECT returns rows as plain objects
affectedRows and changedRows in the result
never build SQL by concatenation

bank.q: Write MongoDB queries to insert three book documents, fetch only title and price for books cheaper than 500, update one document, and delete one. Compare each with its SQL equivalent.
outline: collection.insertMany with BSON documents
find({price: {$lt: 500}}, {title: 1, price: 1, _id: 0})
updateOne with $set and matchedCount/modifiedCount
deleteOne with the ObjectId
filter document versus WHERE clause
no schema means no ALTER TABLE

bank.q: Implement a login endpoint in Express twice: once with express-session and once with a JWT. Show where the credential is stored in each case and how a protected route checks it.
outline: bcrypt hash comparison at login
session: store user id in req.session, cookie carries the id, server-side store
JWT: sign with a secret, send as Authorization: Bearer, verify in middleware
cookie options httpOnly, secure, sameSite
logout: destroy session versus client discards token
revocation is easy for sessions, hard for JWT without a blocklist

bank.q: A route handler calls fs.readFileSync on every request. Analyse what this does to the event loop and to other users, then rewrite it correctly and justify the change.
outline: readFileSync blocks the only JS thread
poll phase cannot run, so other requests queue
timers fire late, health checks fail
readFile with callback, promises or a stream
throughput rises because waiting moves to the OS and thread pool
same reasoning for JSON.parse of huge bodies and long loops

bank.q: Compare SQL injection with NoSQL operator injection. Show one attack on each and evaluate the defence that actually stops it.
outline: SQL: "' OR 1=1 --" in a concatenated query
defence: ? placeholders bind values as data
NoSQL: sending {"$gt": ""} as a password field
defence: type-check and cast, reject object values, schema validation
least-privilege database user
validate at the boundary, never trust req.body

bank.q: A teammate stores the JWT in localStorage because it is simple. Evaluate this choice against an HttpOnly cookie, considering XSS, CSRF and mobile clients.
outline: localStorage is readable by any script in the origin, so XSS steals the token
HttpOnly blocks document.cookie but the browser still sends the cookie, so CSRF appears
sameSite and CSRF tokens counter that
mobile apps have no cookie jar, so header tokens fit better
short expiry plus refresh token limits damage
escaping output and a Content-Security-Policy remove the XSS root cause

bank.q: Explain how Docker and a CI/CD pipeline together remove the phrase "it works on my machine". Describe the stages from git push to a running container and evaluate the risk of deploying the :latest tag.
outline: Dockerfile pins the runtime, OS libs and start command
image built once, container identical on laptop and server
pipeline stages: install, lint, test, build image, push to registry, deploy
secrets injected as environment variables, not baked into the image
:latest is mutable, so a rollback is ambiguous and two servers may run different code
tag by commit SHA and keep the lockfile for exact dependencies

glossary.def: Code that keeps the JavaScript thread busy, so no other callback can run until it returns.
An operation Node hands to the operating system and continues past; the result arrives later through a callback or promise.
The C library that gives Node its event loop, worker thread pool and cross-platform async file and network calls.
libuv's small set of worker threads, four by default, that perform file system, DNS and crypto work away from the main thread.
Schedules a callback to run in the check phase, after the current poll phase finishes.
A stream telling its writer to slow down because the internal buffer is full, so memory does not grow without limit.
A stream helper that connects streams in order and destroys all of them, forwarding errors, when any one fails.
Modules shipped inside Node itself, such as fs, http and path, loaded by bare name with require('fs').
Your own project files, loaded by relative path such as require('./utils') and exported with module.exports.
The folder where npm installs packages; bare-name require() searches it upward from the current file.
Packages needed only for testing, linting or building, which a production install can skip.
The third argument of an Express middleware; calling it hands the request to the next matching function in the chain.
A four-argument Express function (err, req, res, next) that runs only when some earlier middleware called next(err).
A named slot such as :id in a path pattern, readable inside the handler as req.params.id.
The parsed request body; it stays undefined unless express.json() or a similar parser middleware ran first.
A request that can be repeated with the same server state resulting, which is true of GET, PUT and DELETE but not POST.
Binary JSON, the storage format MongoDB uses; ObjectId is its 12-byte identifier type for documents.
An ODM library that adds schemas, casting and validation on top of the plain MongoDB driver.
A deliberately slow password hashing function that adds a random salt, so identical passwords give different hashes.
A cookie the browser sends with requests but hides from document.cookie, so injected script cannot read the session id.
Cross-site request forgery: another site makes the browser send a request that carries the victim's cookie automatically.
Cross-origin resource sharing: response headers that tell the browser which other origins may call your API.
The recipe file listing base image, copied files, dependency install and start command used to build an image.
Configuration passed to a process at run time, such as PORT or DATABASE_URL, so the same image works in every environment.
